Aul
ôl
n. (an awl; a pointed tool for boring; the instrument of the bondservant's permanent covenant)
Old English æl, an awl; the Authorized Version's spelling aul is the older form. The Hebrew martsea' is a boring tool, from a root meaning to pierce.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The law of the Hebrew servant runs six years, and in the seventh he goes out free for nothing. But there is a provision for the man who does not want to go: “if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free: then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever” (Exo 21:5-6). Deuteronomy repeats it: “thou shalt take an aul, and thrust it through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant for ever. And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise” (Deu 15:17). Every element preaches. The servant is legally free; the bondage that follows is chosen, and chosen for love, and the reason is stated aloud before witnesses. The ear is pierced — the organ of hearing and obedience — at the doorpost of the house he is entering for life. And the mark is permanent and visible. Psalm 40:6, quoted of Christ in Hebrews 10:5, says mine ears hast thou opened, literally digged; the Servant who said Lo, I come to do thy will, O God, came under this law voluntarily and for love.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an awl as a pointed instrument for piercing small holes in leather, used by shoemakers, saddlers and other workers in leather.

AWL, n. A pointed instrument for piercing small holes in leather.

It is used by shoemakers, saddlers and other workers in leather.

His master shall bore his ear through with an aul. Ex. xxi.

Key Scripture

Exo 21:6 — "Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever."

Deu 15:17 — "Then thou shalt take an aul, and thrust it through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant for ever. And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise."

Psa 40:8 — "I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart."

Modern Corruption

Freedom is now defined as the absence of binding commitments, so that a permanent, chosen, unbreakable servitude entered for love is unintelligible — which is precisely the shape of Christian discipleship and of marriage.

expand to see more

The bored ear is a scandal to the modern definition of liberty. Our culture defines freedom negatively, as the widest available range of open options, so that every permanent commitment is understood as a subtraction from a man's freedom and every irrevocable one as a kind of self-harm. Exodus 21 describes a man who has just been handed exactly that kind of freedom — the seventh year, out for nothing, no obligation — and who declines it, in public, before judges, because he loves his master and his wife and his children. He then accepts a mark he can never remove. Scripture treats this not as a tragedy but as the highest use a man can make of his liberty, and it is the New Testament's standing self-description for the Christian: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ; ye are not your own, for ye are bought with a price; his servants ye are to whom ye obey. The same logic governs the marriage vow, which is a binding of the will against the future preferences of the will, and church membership, and ordination. A generation taught to keep its options open finds all four incomprehensible and enters none of them wholeheartedly. Christ Himself is the archetype: mine ears hast thou opened; then said I, Lo, I come: I delight to do thy will, O my God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew martsea' (H4836), an awl, a boring tool; karah (H3738), to dig or pierce, of Psalm 40:6; 'ebed 'owlam, a servant for ever.

expand to see more

Hebrew martsea' (H4836) — an awl; used only in the two statements of the bondservant law; Exodus 21:6, Deuteronomy 15:17.

Hebrew karah (H3738) — to dig, to open, to pierce; mine ears hast thou opened, applied to Christ in Hebrews 10:5; Psalm 40:6.

Hebrew 'ebed (H5650) — a servant, a bondman; the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah, and the title Paul takes for himself; Isaiah 42:1, Romans 1:1.

Usage

"“His master shall bore his ear through with an aul” — a permanent mark on a man legally free."

"“Thrust it through his ear unto the door” — the ear, at the doorpost of the house he chose."

"“I delight to do thy will, O my God” — the Servant who came under this law for love."
